source.title: Consistency Regularization on Clean Samples for Learning with Noisy Labels

record.tranche_reason: The paper tests how training on synthetically corrupted labels affects generalization and evaluates a consistency-regularization intervention, but it does not test the original claim's completely random-label memorization setup.
record.gate_note: The paper evaluates noisy-label learning and consistency regularization. Its discussion of the memorization effect and simple patterns is background or interpretation; it does not report a separate direct test of learning order or fitting random labels. Table 1's noisy-label accuracy results bear on V4; rows compare the proposed method with DivideMix and AugDesc.
record.test_reason: The study uses early learning and memorization to motivate noisy-label mitigation. It reports test accuracy, selected-sample MixMatch loss and clean/noisy selection performance, but does not measure memorization of corrupted labels or compare learning trajectories for real and random labels. Declining test accuracy alone does not establish V4's joint claim of perfect training-set fitting and deteriorating generalization.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate: the authors conclude that consistency regularization on samples selected as clean reduces overfitting to easy patterns and improves noisy-label classification. They report improvements over DivideMix and competitive performance against AugDesc, with a shortfall at 80% CIFAR-100 noise. The easy-pattern explanation is their interpretation of selected-sample loss and selection results, rather than a direct test of real-label-first memorization.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies synthetic symmetric label corruption and adds RandAugment-based consistency regularization to DivideMix. It does not reproduce the original random-label memorization experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The results vary with dataset, noise rate, consistency weight λc, and number of augmentation trials I. The paper describes performance as sensitive to λc at 80% noise; at 80% CIFAR-100, AugDesc-WAW outperforms the proposed method.

fits_no_version.finding: Cross-entropy best test accuracy declines from 86.39% to 79.49% to 59.48% on CIFAR-10 and from 61.99% to 47.26% to 22.35% on CIFAR-100 as corruption increases. Training accuracy is not reported.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Increasing symmetric label corruption worsens best test accuracy for a cross-entropy-trained PreAct ResNet-18 at the tested noise rates.

fits_no_version.finding: Sample-selection and consistency methods improve test accuracy under label noise. The proposed I=1 method exceeds DivideMix in all six settings, but AugDesc-WAW performs better at 80% noise on CIFAR-100.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Consistency regularization on samples selected as clean can improve noisy-label classification performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 2 measures MixMatch loss on selected samples with refined and mixed labels; Figures 3–4 measure sample selection counts and clean/noisy classification AUC. These do not measure full training-set memorization or real-versus-noisy label learning order.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Consistency regularization changes selected-sample fitting and the performance of clean-sample selection.

record.problems: No original random-label fitting experiment, no training-error measurements, and no test at 100% noise. Results concern synthetic symmetric corruption on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100. Table 3 caption says 'Attention module' despite the surrounding text describing λc and the proposed method.
record.rows_left_out: No results beyond the 60-row cap. Table 1 results are retained for each method, dataset and noise rate; Table 1's separately reported Last accuracies are omitted to prioritize the main Best accuracy measure. Figure-only curves in Figures 2–4 are not transcribed as rows because exact values are not stated in the text.

untested.parts: Fitting completely random labels to near-zero training error, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Relative time to fit true and random labels, and convergence slowing with increasing corruption.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels and Gaussian-noise inputs.

Perfect fitting of the corrupted training set across a noise sweep and its conjunction with steadily worsening test error through 100% corruption. Only test accuracy at 20%, 50% and 80% corruption is reported.
Whether explicit regularizers prevent random-label fitting and whether removing them harms true-label generalization.
Direct comparison of learning shared real-data patterns before memorizing noisy labels; this ordering is assumed from prior work.

record.verdict_notes: Table 1 values match the record; uncertainties are standard deviations over five noise realizations. Remove the proposed V4 limits_scope verdict: missing training-error measurements are untested evidence, not an observed failure or qualification of V4. All Table 1 entries are method-performance results rather than measurements of the claimed memorization effect.

versions.untested_parts: No experiment trains on completely random labels and reports training error and test error.
No training-time comparison for fitting random versus true labels, or convergence-time sweep by corruption fraction.
No shuffled-pixel, permuted-pixel or Gaussian-noise input experiment.
Training-set fitting error is not reported; the paper reports test accuracy under 20%, 50% and 80% symmetric label noise, not a sweep through all fractions to 100%.
No random-label test of weight decay, dropout or data augmentation, and no experiment removing those regularizers to assess true-label generalization.
No experiment compares learning patterns in real versus random labels over training.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, tested symmetric label-noise rates 20%, 50% and 80%
reader_labels.reason: Table 1 reports test accuracy by corruption rate but no training error, so it cannot establish perfect fitting across the noise sweep (R1–R36).
